utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we get the interpretation? Well, in any event, let's start. Good morning, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Svraka. Can you hear me, Mr. Svraka?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are the microphones switched on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, perhaps you can lean a bit more closer to the microphones. Yes, thank you. I would ask that a particular sequence from Exhibit P1450 be played. And before we do so: Mr. Svraka, did you have an opportunity to watch video footage when you came here to The Hague to prepare for the testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot understand the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that for Markale? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, can you repeat your answer, the beginning? The interpreters could not hear what you said in the beginning. And my question was: Did you see video footage?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Not as a private person; only in court, when they showed me the massacre. I saw it here in court. As a private individual, I didn't watch any of that, and I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. We will play now the sequence starting at 00:54 to the minute 01:50. And we will make certain breaks in between, Mr. Svraka, and I would then ask you questions. Can we please play.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, what do we see here? What location do we see?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: This is in front of the market, in front of the entrance into the market.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you look at this particular photo, do you recognise the scene or any person in that scene?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure. I think I'm the person here in white. I can't see. I don't know. It's as if I were sitting there in a white jacket, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall what you did when you were hit by the blast?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I was standing with colleagues from work. We were smoking cigarettes, and I heard an explosion. I fell on the ground. First, I sort of thought -- what went through my mind was, I'm wounded. And then I touched my face with my hands, and I thought, My head is still there. Judges, maybe this sounds incredible, but I did not see anything when I opened my eyes. I started breathing, and I thought, Well, I can breathe. I tried to move my legs. I couldn't move them. And that was it, until they threw me into the back of a car. And then I opened my eyes. I held on to the front seat. I saw the driver walking around the car, and he said, Don't worry, Grampa. I was a Grampa even then. I had a six-month-old grandchild who got killed. I asked the driver where we were going, what hospital. There were two hospitals, the then Military Hospital and the Kosevo Centre. I had worked in Kosevo for 10 years, and they told me to go to Kosevo. The driver went with me. When I entered Kosevo, I was half conscious and half in shock. When I entered Kosevo, there's like a tunnel, like a passageway. I personally worked in that tunnel before. I saw the nurses holding two bottles. Now, what was that, was it blood or whatever the name of the other thing is? I saw a doctor walking among the people there. There were lots of dead and wounded. I heard the doctor saying, It's impossible to work this way. Try to get some order here. Twice, I said to the nurses or doctors, whatever, I said, I'm cold, I'm cold. I heard scissors cutting my trousers on the right side. I didn't see who was doing that. I woke up in the Intensive Care Department. There were tiles all the way up to the ceiling. That was upstairs. I saw wounded persons, sick persons, all over the place. No one was crying, nothing. Later on, I just saw that they were plugged in to electricity, because when there would be a power cut, I saw that everybody would get all worked up, and they tried to somehow get them back to the electric current.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Svraka. Can we now proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When we stop here briefly, do you recall in which car you were transported? Do you have any memory of that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I don't know. In a Golf, that's what I said in some statement, but I couldn't see anything until I got into the car, and I'm not a driver myself. I know that I was in the car by myself and that they sort of put me in this way [indicates]. I was lying on the right-hand side, and I leaned on the front seat with my left hand. What car it was, I really cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we proceed, please, with the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Svraka, this door that we see here, what kind of door is it? What does it lead into?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: It should be the door leading to the shopping centre. The street was called Vase Miskina before. There are steps there, this is a tram line. I'm somewhere around here, about two metres away from the door. I was standing there with my colleagues. And that's where the main road was and the main market, and you can always find something there. People were buying and selling. You could always get something to survive there. There was no transportation. You always had to walk. If people had a bicycle, then that would be the best kind of transportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you say you were at the door, near the door. Were you to the left or to the right of the door, when you look at this photo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Viewed from here, to the left of the door. There's sort of something here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's sufficient from this video. And, Your Honours, it's already an exhibit, so we don't need to do anything about it. Your Honours, that concludes the examination-in-chief. There are no further exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, it's now for you to cross-examine Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Svraka.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to pay my respects to you, in view of everything that you have lived through. Therefore, I'm not going to put many questions to you, just a few. Tell me, were you under work obligation all the time or were you a member of a war unit for a while?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Work obligation started perhaps a month or two after the war broke out. I did not spend a single hour in the army. I was under work obligation all the time, and I also went digging. When there was this work obligation, they'd come and they'd say -- well, I mean, as for among the people who stayed at the company, say five people would have to go and dig canals, trenches, whatever. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation. That's why I'm pausing. Tell me where di you live at the time, what was your address?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Same place. However, the street changed. Ragibinda [phoen] 70, Buvljakov Potok, that was my address then. The municipality was Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you go to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: At Zuc, for the most part. I also went to Igman for 20 days. I was at Igman, and then I came back and I was off for 10 days. During those 10 days, I went to the market. That was the last time I walked, ever. We were digging above Grbavica, Stup, Zuc, I mean all of that. I remember I would come to this Orahov Brijeg, as it was called. I think that that is the farthest point I got to from my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it better or easier to be in these work platoons and to be under work obligation or was it easier to go to the front-line? Did people prefer work obligation? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: As soon as the shooting started, I reported to the local commune, and I asked to be deployed somewhere, because if you were not deployed anywhere, you didn't dare walk about town. This is exactly what they said to me: Grampa, we don't have enough weapons even for young men, let alone for you. They wrote up some kind of document for me, saying that I could move about freely, because at first, in the company, no one really went to work for the first 10 or 20 days. We didn't dare to because of the snipers. Afterwards, we, the elderly, usually -- well, the company was in Pofalici, in a high-rise building near Grbavica, and we started getting water out of the basements. There were about 500 workers there at the time. We went there to repair roofs, and then -- actually, I was working on a construction site, as it were, and a courier came and said, Five men have to go tonight, and you choose who it's going to be. We did it in alphabetical order. Five men were selected, and my next-door neighbour was told that he should go and I did not go, and another colleague said he -- I don't know, he worked with trucks, he did something, and he said, Is there anyone to replace me, And I'll replace that person some other time. And I said, I will go -- I will go to replace you. He's my neighbour. Because when you go to dig trenches, then you go together, and on your way back, whatever. And then I sort of thought, I prefer going with a neighbour. If something happens, he will help him and I will help me, and I was with him throughout work obligation. And the third day, when I woke up in hospital, shelling could be heard in Jahorinski Potok. That's what people were saying, too. I knew that area because I built two-weekend cottages there. I was a mason, so I did some private work of my own almost every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about Jahorinski Potok, you were talking about the NATO bombing of the Serb positions after that shell?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that could be heard in the hospital. I heard someone say, They've started bombing them. That's what was heard in Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those documents stating that you could move about freely or that you were engaged somewhere, did that help you move about more freely in town?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Beforehand, if you went to town, some people from the army would just come and pick you up on the street and they take you out to dig, and people at your home wouldn't know where you were and what happened to you. And I was in this work unit, work obligation. The company was called Herzegovina. So I was assigned somewhere, so I wasn't just hanging out in the street. So, yes, I could move about freely in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, was that the first time that you were in Markale or did you go to the same place often?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Markale is an area where I passed through very often. I had a sister who lived in the Old City. I had a garden of 200, 300 square metres where I lived, and then I'd collect some vegetables or fruit, and then I'd take that to my sister who lived in town. I mostly went to Zuc to get timber, because timber saved me during the war. I could get food and oil for it. I waited to get salt for ages once, so I didn't want to go to town very often. I was supposed to mail a letter to my brother in Germany. And my sister's neighbour was supposed to go, although that neighbour actually never went. And I gave my brother the letter to read only when he returned much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away from you was this explosion? So you were between the explosion and the door, right, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Three or four metres, it wasn't further than that, on my right-hand side. It is marked to this day. I never passed there by car to this day without saying, That is my shell. That's what I call it. Three or four metres, not more than that. Two of my colleagues were standing there with me. We were standing by this place, and we were all smoking cigarettes. They were facing the facade, the wall of the shopping centre, whereas I was facing them. Probably -- I don't know. As I said, I didn't see anything, but probably because of the detonation, they probably hit the walls, their heads hit the walls, and I fell on the pavement. This is being repeated every year in world news and BH news, every year on the day when that massacre occurred, so I see it. In hospital, I heard that those two colleagues got killed. One of them was a colleague from my brigade. I thought that we were in the same brigade, because the army also had a brigade at the construction site, also a brigadier there. A colleague from a brigade, he was actually an unskilled worker, but I was a master craftsman. And, anyway, this colleague got killed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were closer to the point of explosion than you were -- than they were; it seems that way?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: Half a metre, perhaps half a metre closer to the shell. I don't know, so just think of what the distance is. I mean, all of us were standing within a single square metre, all three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear something before the explosion, itself?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. I just heard the explosion. And before that, we were talking. One of them was looking for flour. The other one was selling jam, or honey, or whatever it was. We were smoking cigarettes. We hadn't smoked, say, more than half a cigarette. I didn't hear anything before the explosion, except for the conversation that the three of us were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were four shells about 300 or 400 metres away from you. Did you hear them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: No. I heard one shell. I fell. After that, I don't know. I don't know when the rest fell. I think that was the first one, because usually there is commotion after the first shell falls, and people seek shelter somewhere. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, where were you hit by shrapnel? How far did the shrapnel go?

utterances.speaker: ISMET SVRAKA
utterances.text: I didn't feel anything until the men came there to bandage me. The left leg was amputated above the knee. The right leg, I mean, that, they cleaned it for a month. It's like cleaning a ham. They cut a piece, and then if it's not good, then they go on cutting, and that went on for a month. My right ankle was wounded, and two of my toes were removed. And then underneath the foot, practically, my foot was almost cut off, but then they managed to sew that up. When I first woke up in Kosevo, when they asked me, How are you doing, Grampa, does it hurt, and I said, I have a stomachache, that was a bit funny. One leg was missing, the other one was bandaged, and I'm saying I have a stomachache. They touched it. It started swelling. They didn't even see that I was hit by shrapnel in the abdominal area, too. Then they may have sewed that up too. But my stomach started swelling up. They took me for surgery. They brought me some shrapnel like half a cube of sugar. I kept it for a year or two. I don't even know how it got mislaid after that. I was wounded in the stomach. Seven days later -- oh, yes, it was Milosevic who did the operation. I can't remember his first name. They came a week later, and I again said that I felt pain in my stomach. I guess the tube got stuck or something. The doctor took the tube out, and a litre of blood sputtered all over the doctor, and he said, Oh, we'll have to clean him again. Then again I had to be operated on. While I was at surgery, whatever it was called -- I know it was called surgery, the Surgical Department, that's where I was first. And after that, I was transferred to this place called Abdominal Surgery, that's what they call it. And then I had these medical persons coming from the Orthopaedics Department, and they wanted to bandage my leg, and that wasn't enough material. And then from Abdominal Surgery, I was transferred to Orthopaedics. The doctor who cut off my leg, who performed the first surgery, Gavranka Petanovic [phoen] was his name, and he kept saying that I have a nice name. Only later on, I heard that his name was Ismet, so that gave me a bit more strength. I have some shrapnel here in my head as well. About three years ago they took an X-ray, and they said, You're doing fine Grampa, don't worry. And then here in the stomach -- I listened to the doctor, and he said, I should have taken away half of his intestines. How much he did get out, I don't know. I just know that I have stomach trouble to this day. I mean, I have to eat more often, but, well, I don't know, it bothers me if I eat, I don't feel very well. That's what I have to say about my wounding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Once again, I would like to pay my respects to you, in view of everything that you've been through. I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic, and thank you, Mr. Svraka. Do you have any re-direct examination, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, nothing arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Svraka. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and this Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go, and please have a safe journey back to home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would kindly ask you to invite me again when Mladic is here. If that's the last thing I do, I would like to come here and see him in court, brought before justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. May I now go home? It's over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Goodbye. Goodbye, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell us who the next witness is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Hamill. And I hope he's already in the building, because we, of course, thought it would take -- Mr. Karadzic would have an hour. So I hope he's already in the building. Perhaps we can make a short break, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we break for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break for five minutes. We'll resume at 20 to 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.32 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Hamill. Could you kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, could you actually, please, tell us your full name, and give us your rank, in fact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: My name is John Hamill. I'm a lieutenant-colonel in the Irish Army, in the Artillery Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, this is also not your first appearance before a Chamber of this Tribunal. You've given evidence on two previous occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. I gave evidence in two cases, the Galic case and the Kordic/Cerkez case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in preparation for your testimony here today, have you had a chance to review the transcript of your evidence in the Galic case and the exhibits that were discussed during the course of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a result of that review, did you have any additions, or corrections, or clarifications you felt you needed to make?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably, you might have been told, but, Mr. Hamill, because you and Ms. Edgerton speak the same language, which should be translated into French as well as B/C/S, if you could put a pause between the question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if today I was to ask you the same questions that you were asked during the course of your Galic testimony, would your answers also be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, please, Your Honours, could I have the transcript of Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill's evidence in the Galic case, which is 65 ter 10336, entered as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll now read a summary of that written evidence. Lieutenant-Colonel John Hamill served in Sarajevo as a United Nations Military Observer from May to July 1993. During this period, he was deployed in areas both north and south of the city, working exclusively in Sarajevo Romanija Corps or SRK-held territory. His duties and functions at that time included monitoring weapons use and deployment, as well as carrying out a liaison function at SRK Command. The witness observed that the SRK used their artillery -- pardon me, their artillery in a militarily non-conventional way, in the sense that they very rarely moved. He recalls that not a day passed without a shooting or shelling. On one particular day, UN observers counted 3.610 outgoing shells from VRS positions over a 12-hour period. The witness described the use of sniping as an instrument of terror. In his view, there was sufficient control by the political and military authorities to have stopped sniping if they wished. In his capacity as liaison officer at Lukavica, Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill frequently protested to SRK officials over incidents of shelling and sniping as reported from his UNMO colleagues. He observed that SRK officers had the capacity to immediately contact the relevant brigade commanders concerning certain incidents. In February 1994, Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill returned to Sarajevo as technical adviser to a United Nations team tasked with investigating the shelling at Markale Market. He drafted the report on the investigation and collated the related annexures. During the course of the team's investigations, the witness had occasion to speak with the Bosnian Serb Army's designated liaison for the team, Colonel Cvjetkovic, whom he understood to be the commander of the SRK Artillery Regiment. In the course of this interview, Colonel Cvjetkovic said that in the previous year, they had fired 30.000 to 40.000 rounds into the city, and asked Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill why they were so concerned about one round when they had fired so many. The UN team came to the conclusion that the explosion of 5 February 1994 was caused by a conventional, factory-produced 120-millimetre high-explosive mortar bomb which detonated upon impact with the ground, fired from the north-north-east. Six potential firing locations along that axis were identified, two on the ABiH or Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina side and four on Bosnian Serb-held territory. This witness also examined two shell craters in Dobrinja in 2001. Those related to the shelling of a football-match in the area on 1 June 1993. On the basis of his investigations, he concluded that rounds were fired from the area of Toplik, an SRK heavy weapons location where the witness, himself, had been posted during his tour in the city. And that concludes the summary of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, I have just a few questions in relation to the written evidence that was filed and which we've spoken about, just some areas of clarification, and I'll go through those now. First, in that written evidence, at pages 6063, 6218, 6230 and 6231, you referred to a band of irregulars, which you described as so-called Chetniks led by one Vasilije Vidovic, known as Vasko. You said he regularly impeded UNMO movement in areas across the city, and you said further, based on what you were told by your interpreter at the time, Vasko was under control of a General Josipovic, who commanded various brigades on the north part of the city. You said, in particular at page 6218 and 6219, that the object of his band was to spread terror throughout the area and prevent entry into specified areas to the north and east of Sarajevo. And also at page 6219, you noted that you were of the view that they were used -- that band was used as a tool by authorities to conduct operations which could be disowned; in other words, black operations. So, in fact, you had a lot of information about this band of Chetniks, and I'm wondering, other than information you received from your interpreter at the time, what you base this on. Could you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly. Our teams in the north part of the city had a lot of trouble from this particular band, and as I say, so-called Chetniks. They were impeded from entering various parts of our area of operations around Vogosca, Rajlovac, Radava, and further east. This was done particularly towards the end of June and the beginning of and middle of July 1993, when teams were specifically stopped by him. His band was quite small, but travelled widely within areas controlled by four or five different VRS brigades. Therefore, they clearly had freedom of movement in that area. They stopped UNMOs, they threatened UNMOs. On more than one occasion, they opened fire in the direction of UNMOs. And as I say, my understanding was that he was under control of a General Josipovic, who apparently had responsibility for the brigades to the north of the city. I personally never met General Josipovic, nor saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you ever meet this Vasko?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I met Vasko on a number of occasion. Mr. Vidovic stopped a patrol that I was on when I was trying to get to that part of the city on the 20th of July, 1993, and attempted to place explosives on my vehicle. When he was persuaded not to so do, he instructed us to leave the area and not come back. However, we had business to do in the Poljine area north of the city, so we went to that area by a different route. And there, Mr. Vidovic arrived with his team and opened fire as they drove into the farmyard where we were operating at the time. So, yes, I have had occasion to actually meet Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did anything happen after they opened fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: They placed my colleague and myself against a wall for execution. However, our interpreter very bravely, and subsequently he received a force commander's commendation for it, spoke on a very serious basis, clearly, with Mr. Vidovic, who decided then to take us to the brigade headquarters in Vogosca for execution in front of the brigade commander. On the way there, I surreptitiously notified our headquarters that this was happening, and when we got to Vogosca, after some time we were released by the brigade commander. Clearly, we were not executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you, following your release, inform anyone within the SRK structures as to what had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: We certainly did. We spoke to the brigade headquarters and also to the SRK headquarters in order to get our equipment back, because he had, of course, taken our equipment when he had captured us. This proved to be fruitless in the end. He had taken a vehicle, he had taken flak-jackets, helmets, ID cards, various other items.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just moving further in your evidence to pages 6138 and 6163, you specifically recalled a day - and I mentioned it in the summary of that evidence - when UNMOs recorded 3.610 rounds in a 12-hour period outgoing from the Bosnian Serb side. Now, it's not clear, and perhaps you recall. Was this outgoing from the north or south side of the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: This was all outgoing from the north side of the city, and it took place on the 22nd of July, 1993, which was two days after the events which I've just related in relation to Mr. Vidovic. And it was only afterwards that I put together the two pieces of information; that he was attempting to keep UNMOs out of that part of the city, where the artillery was based, and the shelling which took place shortly afterwards, because clearly it took a great deal of time to assemble the ammunition and prepare the fire plans for that day. So from my professional experience now, I would say that they were preparing that attack well in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to turn to a document you referred to in your Galic testimony. It has the -- it's been exhibited here as P1441. It's a 64-page document that perhaps has some pages out of order, and I thought you might be able to assist the Trial Chamber in their consideration of this document. And, Your Honours, given that there may be some pages out of order, with everyone's permission I propose to provide Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill with a hard copy of this as well. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means. I take it there's no opposition from the Defence, either. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just take a moment, Lieutenant-Colonel, to flip through that document. And have you had an opportunity to review this document also in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: This is a complete report on the explosion into the market place -- bombing of Markale of the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who wrote that complete report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The essence of the report was actually drafted by myself and confirmed by the other members of the team. This was for the actual report. Now, there are other documents also attached which I was not responsible for, which were, for example, the daily situational report for Sector Sarajevo, and parts of the actual analysis which were done by our adjutant chef.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I wonder, Lieutenant-Colonel, if you could, referring to the numbers stamped at the top right corner of each page, explain to the Trial Chamber how they should understand this document and how it's structured. For example, you referred to the essence of the report, and the actual report. Where might we find that in this range of pages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The essence of the report starts at 1024713, goes through 14, 15, 16, and then the annexures to that start, obviously, at 17, and so on and so forth. It gives a list of witnesses. It does the technical analysis in Annex C. It gives the methodology. It gives those who conducted the individual analyses, and when they did, and what the results were. It talks about the findings in relation to the weapon, to the bearing, to the angle of descent. It gives conclusions, which were quite sparse, in actual fact. And then it goes into the individual reports of different analysts, members of the team, including myself, which we'll find at 1024729. Other annexes include diagrams and drawings of the area where the bomb exploded in Markale, and firing tables which were used to determine the possible ranges, and I have to emphasise that it's possible ranges to where the weapon was fired from. It gives a summary of the testimony of general witness as opposed to technical witnesses. And, in effect, that's really it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I wonder now if we might be able to turn to e-court and the version of the document in front of you on the screen, because I'd like to ask you one question in relation to e-court page 9, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just so you can refer to the document in front of you, it has the "R1024713" number which you referred to just a couple of seconds ago at page 21, line 9. Do you see paragraph 4 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note that paragraph 4 says: "Liaison officers from the parties were permitted to maintain contact with the investigation team, but not to participate in the investigation." What was the rationale behind not permitting representatives of the warring factions to participate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Very simply put, this was a United Nations investigation. This was not an investigation being conducted by the authorities of either the Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it would not have been appropriate to have had members from the warring factions on that team. They were permitted to maintain contact with the investigation team for reasons of transparency and openness, and clearly it was not in the United Nations' interest to have hidden goings on, as it were. It was in the UN's interest that this investigation should be seen by both sides to be open, fair, transparent and legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to another document now, please, 65 ter 10053, page 2. And that will not be given to you in hard copy. It should appear on the screen in front of you. Could you please go over to page 2 in the B/C/S version. Make it page 3, I think, in the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you also, Lieutenant-Colonel, seen this document in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise it, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is the statement which I made on the 18th of September, 2001, following an investigation that I conducted at the behest of the Tribunal on explosions which took place in Dobrinja in May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I actually just have one question in relation to this statement, and it arises from something that appears in paragraph 2, the last sentence. You note there -- or paragraph 2 reads that the prismatic compass you used to take bearings was calibrated to match the map. First of all, could you explain to us what a prismatic compass is and then how you calibrated the compass to match the map?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: A prismatic compass is just a very rugged compass which is used by artillery officers to take bearings; that is, to find the direction from one place, where you're standing, to another place. It had to be calibrated because there are always variations within compasses. And in order to calibrate it, you need to find two locations which you know on the map, and, therefore, you match, as it were, the compass to the map; not the map to the compass, but the compass to the map. So I calibrated it in order that the bearings that I took on the ground would be relatable to the bearings on the map. Compass bearings are inherently tricky. They are inherently inaccurate because of the construction of the compass and also possibly because of the composition of the area in which the bearings are being taken. There may be steel or iron, for example, located close which would put a compass off. So it's important that the compass should be calibrated so that an accurate bearing is taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to take a back, then, from this to the investigation you conducted in February 1994, did you similarly calibrate the compass during the course of that earlier investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honours. And I would at this point like to ask that the associated exhibits for Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill, which have not otherwise been admitted into evidence, be marked as Prosecution exhibits, and I could go through those at this moment or deal with them with my colleagues, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The only exhibit that has been admitted seems to be General Rose's book. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Following General Rose's book, there's P1440, which, on the original notification which was filed some time ago, Your Honours, is listed as 65 ter 09623.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that also admitted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then, of course, as I've indicated, P1441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: P1441 is the 9630?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, of course, before I sit down, I would ask that this statement that Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill has just spoken about be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we do that. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one final clarification. The last item, which bears the 65 ter number 19537, you tendered it as a kind of courtesy because it was discussed during the cross-examination. The witness confirmed that he heard such rumours, but he said the content of this document is utter nonsense. So on what basis can you admit? This is an article. It was sort of an interview appearing in the news media, and to which the witness said the content of which is nonsense. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And, indeed, Your Honour, my apologies. It was listed there as a courtesy as part of the total number of exhibits dealt with during his earlier testimony, but that's not one I would be seeking to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not our practice to admit a third person's interview appearing in the news media. So following that practice, we are not minded to admit that one. More than that, the witness confirmed that he the heard rumours, and he gave his observation in his testimony, so there's no need to admit it. So excluding that, and the other associated exhibits will be admitted and given numbers in due course by the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic, would you start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. -- Dr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the outset, I would like to express my gratitude that you -- that you have agreed to meet with the Defence team. Everything is turned on on my side. Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wish to say thank you for meeting with the Defence team and enabling us to shed light on certain concepts which, in turn, will enable this examination to run smoothly. Let me ask you: Is it true that whenever something happened, like sniping or artillery incidents or shelling, you were informed by the BH side by radio, and then you were able to intervene with the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is not strictly correct. We were generally informed by our own headquarters, which was the United Nations headquarters based in the PTT building in Sarajevo. So we weren't informed by the BH side; we were informed by our own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are correct, of course. I had, in fact, said you were informed by the Papa side. And to make it clear what "Papa" means, that means your crews, your teams, on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were able to contact the liaison officer of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and demand a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were times when liaison officers tried to obtain a cease-fire and succeeded, and sometimes they refused, explaining that they were returning fire in response to prior attacks by the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, regarding the incident of the 1st of June, 1993, involving a football game, you had not received any request from the Papa side for the VRS attack to stop; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm not aware that such a thing did or did not happen. At the time that this attack occurred, I was actually well to the east of the city in the general area of Mokro, so I was not aware precisely what was happening inside in Dobrinja or other parts of the city. It may have been that there were contacts made or there may not have been. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the case of this incident, there was no mixed investigation commission set up for this incident in Dobrinja, because those mixed commissions were formed for the first time to deal with the Markale incident; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: There were no mixed commissions at any stage anywhere that I'm aware of, including the investigation into Markale I of the 5th of February of 1994. There were investigations conducted by UNMOs or by other parts of the United Nations organisation into incidents which occurred throughout the four years of the hostilities in that general area, but I'm not aware of any mixed commissions which took in personnel from the warring parties. In the case of the Markale explosion, due to the high profile of the event, a decision was made far above my pay level that there should be contact and liaison with the warring parties. This is not a mixed commission. This was a UN investigation. In relation to the Dobrinja episode, it was just one more in a series of attacks in the Sarajevo area in which civilians died. There was no requirement that I'm aware of for a special investigation into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the 26th of March, 2002, at the Galic trial on page 6764: "To the best of my knowledge, no mixed commission was set up at that time for either of these incidents." [In English] "The first such comission that I remember specifically was that which occurred after the Markale shelling on the 5th of February, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really sorry, but in the transcript that I have from the Galic case, there is no page 6764, and I wonder if I could just ask Dr. Karadzic to have another look for the page reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 6164. I apologise. Probably I was misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It could be 65 ter 10336, and the page 107. [Interpretation] Could we call that up in e-court, page 7. Line 9 begins the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Lieutenant-Colonel, that the Serbian side always insisted they wanted to take part in investigations, and that they would not recognise the results unless the Serbian experts were involved?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Dobrinja and in Markale, in all these incidents where you conducted your investigation, the Muslim side also conducted its own investigation, and the Serbian side was the only one that was not involved and did not have any investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm aware that in the case of the Markale incident, the Presidency side certainly conducted an investigation. I am not aware whether or not the Serb side conducted an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you investigated two craters in Dobrinja, shown to you by Ismet Fazlic -- in fact, you looked at these two craters after the war, and they were shown to you by Mr. Ismet Fazlic, who was an eye-witness and, I believe, also organiser and referee at the football-match. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I investigated those craters in 2001, which was several years after the explosions in case, obviously. And it was Mr. Fazlic who showed us where the shell -- where the bombs exploded or the shells exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The crater was filled with a red substance, like plastic, to cover it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not specifically to cover it. It was filled with a red substance -- the individual marks were filled with a red substance, which was plasticised, which preserved, largely, the craters intact. And the investigation I conducted was on the basis that the marks were kept intact by this red substance. This was the case with one of the two locations. It was not the case with the other. It was not possible to be very specific with the second crater, but it was possible to be fairly specific with the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we look at 65 ter 10053. 10053, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "The craters are old, and both are filled for protection with a red substance. However, this has a certain impact on the craters." I suppose there was no unauthorised -- there was no unauthorised tampering with the crater, and the red substance is the only intervention. "Crater 1 is better preserved than Crater 2. The interventions were such that it was not possible to determine at this time whether the craters were made by a gun or a mortar." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that the filling of the crater with the red substance affected the reliability or, rather, the usability of the craters to determine the origin and the type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, we don't. On the contrary, I would say that the filling of the marks with the plasticised substance preserved it over a period of eight years and enabled me to do a reasonable job of determining from where and what type of weapon was used.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I was led to ask this question by something you said in the Galic trial, page 59 in the previous document, as the transcript of 25 March 2002. Page 59, bottom of the page. [In English] "Q. Now, you said in respect to the analysis that you did on the 18th of June last year -- 18th of September last year, I beg your pardon -- "A. Yes. "Q. -- the craters you saw were probably from a gun. "A. Yes. A howitzer. "Q. And also possibly from a medium-calibre mortar? "A. That is a possibility, yes." But: "You must bear in mind that the craters had been filed with this red plastic substance, so it was not possible to determine exactly the conditions --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page. "... the condition they were in when they were fresh."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not have the elements to determine with certainty whether, apart from filling with red substance, there were any other interventions on the craters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: When I examined the area, it was clear that the surrounding substrate was untouched for a very, very long period of time. It was quite clear that the marks which were on the substrate were practically unchanged over that period. And as I said, the red plasticised substance had the -- had actually preserved the craters in the condition in which they were originally, it would appear to me. I saw no evidence that there had been any changes made to the concrete in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But neither did you have evidence there had been no tampering before the filling with the red substance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. But it would have been very difficult to have tampered with the area in such a way that it didn't show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they inform you when they had filled the craters with this red substance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you have told us that the best time for examining an incident is the moment after the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, it's time to take a break. We'll break for 30 minutes, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that an investigation ideally should be conducted the moment after the incident, do you agree that the site, the crime scene, can be altered either artificially or naturally due to the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is quite clear that a crime scene can be altered either artificially or naturally due to the passage of time, because clearly in a situation like this, which is open to the elements, there will be a certain amount of wear, particularly given the Bosnian weather, which involves a lot of snow, frost, ice, and so on, which certainly will damage surfaces which are left untreated. But as I indicated, the fact that the red plasticised substance had, at some stage relatively early on, been placed on the markings, they were fairly well preserved. And, further, I have seen photographs which purport to be those craters in their original condition, taken almost immediately after the incident in question, and the marks bear a striking resemblance to those which are still there to this day. I can, in fact, see no inconsistency between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to establish whether it would have been important to determine when that red substance was poured onto the traces, but fine. In view of all this, it was made impossible to determine the origin of the projectile and the type of weapon that fired it. It was impossible to determine whether it was a cannon or a mortar; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was not impossible to determine the origin of the projectile. It was very, very possible to determine the direction from which the round arrived in on the ground. It was very clear, it was very obvious, and there is no ambiguity about it. It came, as I said in the report, from a specific direction. As to whether it was a mortar bomb or a shell from a gun or a howitzer, it is much more difficult. My personal view is that it was a medium -- or a light- to medium-type shell. It may have been a medium mortar, as I indicated, but my belief is that it was from a shell from around 105 to 130 millimetres, looking at the effect on the ground. And also looking at the original photograph, it seems to be quite clear to me, if not to others, that it was from a gun or a howitzer, which is, in effect, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the trajectory of a projectile from a gun or a howitzer, that is to say, artillery weapon, is different from a trajectory of a projectile fired by a mortar, and that to determine the direction and especially the distance, it would be crucial to determine the type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Firstly, it is simply not possible to determine the distance that the round has been fired from. That is simply impossible. It cannot be done in the case of any weapon, regardless of what you might hear. However, it is certainly possible to determine, normally, whether it was a gun/howitzer or a mortar. There is a difference in the trajectory between a gun and a mortar, clearly. A mortar is fired at an angle above 45 degrees. A gun is, effectively, a flat trajectory weapon which may be fired at maybe 10, maybe 20 degrees elevation, so it's a round coming in flat. However, a howitzer, which has most of the characteristics of a gun, can also be fired at a high angle there, which means at above 45 degrees, so, in effect, a howitzer round can come in on the same trajectory as a mortar bomb. The howitzer can also be fired flat, like a gun. What this means is that a mortar or a howitzer round can come in from behind high cover, whereas a gun cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we call up in e-court P1053.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are aware that the French investigating team conducted an investigation and provided their findings; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: This appears to be a Canadian Forces Military Police investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is one thing that I find confusing. Could you focus on Crater 1 and Crater 2. We can all read these: [In English] "Splinter pattern indicates mortar, minimum calibre 81, bearing to original fire, 143 degrees," that makes 2.500 mils. "Due to the macadam, there is no fuse furrow, so that angle of descent and range cannot be determined." [Interpretation] With the second crater, everything is the same, except that the degree is 138, which makes 2.420 mils. Thus, these UNPROFOR investigators found that it was a mortar of at least 81-millimetre calibre; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see page 57 of this document. And I advise the parties to look at other conclusions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is part of the investigating material of the UNPROFOR based on the information received from Din ko Bakal from the Dobrinja Brigade Staff. Can we see -- yes, we can see it now: [In English] "I was about 60 to 70 metres from the place where the shell landed. That happened about 10.25 to 10.30 a.m. I was in the apartment at the first floor, from where I was able to see the playground very well. When I heard the detonations, I thought these were mortar shells with 82 calibre. However, later we found parts of a mortar shell, and they were 60 millimetres calibre." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this becomes more and more muddled? Based on the fragments that were collected, it seems to be a round of 63 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I don't agree that it's more and more muddled. You must remember, Dr. Karadzic, that there was an awful lot of mortar bombs of all descriptions being fired at the Dobrinja area during the period from April 1992 up until the end of May 1993 and onwards, so it's quite possible that there were bits of 60-millimetre mortar bombs lying around. Again, my opinion, as I said earlier on, is that it was actually a shell, perhaps 122 millimetres, from a howitzer, not from a mortar. I may be wrong on that, but you asked for my professional opinion, and that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that a mortar of 63 millimetres is practically considered small arms? It can be carried on your person and it can be fired from anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I could not possibly consider a mortar of 60 millimetres, not 63, to be small arms. Small arms consist of rifles, pistols, submachine guns and the like. But, yes, a 60-millimetre mortar can be carried on a person, is designed to be carried by a person, and can be fired by one individual. I wouldn't like to carry it too far, though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the transcript, it's recorded that I said "small arms." I said "some sort of personal weapon." That's not what I said. Perhaps that caused the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So a 60-millimetre mortar would be about 50 centimetres, half a metre, that is, in length; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: A little bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 6 of the same document. Para 14: "Around 0945 hours on the 4th of July, 1993, a copy of the map of Dobrinja was received from UNPROFOR officials, a copy of which is attached as Annex 1. The map shows that the soccer game was held in a location surrounded on three sides by buildings (west, east, and south)." And it was open only facing north: "In addition, it was explained that there are Bosnian mortars located outside the hospital approximately 500 metres from the soccer location. However, these were not observed during this visit to Dobrinja."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not aware whether that is correct or not. However, what I can say is that it is irrelevant if there were buildings on three sides, four sides, or no sides, because the reality is that a mortar bomb or a howitzer shell comes in normally at a steep angle of descent. Therefore, it can be used to go behind buildings. In relation to Bosnian mortars located, I'm not aware where the hospital is, nor am I aware whether or not there were mortars there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 65 ter 10053. 10053.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3, you provided information to the OTP in 2001, where it says: "Crater 2 is not so well preserved." The most one can say, looking at that crater, in view of its shape, is that the shell seems to have been fired from the same direction as the shell that created Crater 1?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to go back to the previous document, P1053, and to look at the same paragraphs where the UNPROFOR team made conclusions about Crater 1 and Crater 2. That's page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we see what their conclusions are with regard to the azimuth, and also they say that the angle of descent could not have been determined. Please look further down. Look at the conclusions. Paragraph 2: "The minimum angle of descent for 81-millimetre, 120-millimetre mortars is 45.71 degrees. At that angle, the minimum range is 1.120 metres for 81-millimetre mortar and 1.340 metres for 120-millimetre mortar." So their conclusion is that the shells only could have been fired from the Serbian side, that that is indicated by both bearings. "At the minimum range, the mortars were 300 metres south of Lukavica Barracks." First of all, I would like to ask you the following: On the basis of what did this French investigator determine the minimum angle of descent -- Canadian, rather? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I believe he was Canadian. Certainly the military police investigation were Canadians. Whether or not they were United Nations, I do not know. What I would say is that in order to determine minimum angles of descent, you have to look at the range tables for the specific weapon. Now, the general weapon in use in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as in most of Eastern and -- Eastern Europe, would be the 82-millimetre weapon, which is produced by the former Soviets. The 81-millimetre weapon tends to be a Western weapon, often French made. Similarly, the 120-millimetre mortar tends to be a Western weapon, and the former Soviet equipment is 122 millimetres. So there is a difference. You have to examine the specific range tables, and this is one of the problems that we have seen in a number of investigations, that incorrect range tables were used to calculate possible ranges for different incidents. In this case, again, as I said, I am not convinced that it actually was a mortar. The angle of descent -- the minimum angle of descent indicates that it could have been a mortar, but, equally, that it could be a howitzer. I have no argument with that. In terms of the bearing to the origin of fire, you'll note that the team in question came up, apparently, with two different bearings, one of 2420 mils and one of 2500 mils, which would indicate the two weapons fired at some distance from each other. As I said, in my investigation, I found that I had a fairly specific bearing for the first crater, but for the second crater, it was more indeterminate, but that it was generally from the same direction. This would -- this would agree with my findings. I had not seen this particular report before I conducted my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let us now clarify matters. The minimum angle is what the investigators have stated here. What is the maximum angle, on the assumption that it is a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It depends very much on what type of mortar it is. It depends very much on the charge used. The maximum would be where you use the maximum number of supplementary charges. If I could explain to the Court that a mortar bomb is not fired with a fixed [Realtime transcript read in error "mixed"] amount of charge. There is a basic charge, a primer, which is the minimum charge, and then horseshoes or little sashays are added to the base of the bomb to increase the range so that if a bomb is fired, for example, at an angle of 70 degrees elevation, there could be a very wide variation in the range, because depending on the number of sashays or horseshoes attached, the round will go up a certain distance into the air before it, as it were, turns over and begins to fall, so the more charges there are on it, the further it will go. At 45 degrees, 45 degrees is the maximum range for any specific charge. So at 45 degrees on maximum charge, you have maximum range for any particular mortar, and what that is depends very much on the weapon, itself, and the type of bomb which is used in it. In other words, I cannot say, in this particular case, without range tables and without knowing specifically what weapon and what charges were used. Neither can anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that the transcript says "does not fire," whereas you said "does fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that right? Please have a look at the transcript, line six: [In English] "The maximum --"

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In line 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... was not fired" --

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry. In line 8, if I could change that, please. It's not fired with a fixed amount of charge, not "mixed." The first word on line 8 should be "fixed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we simplify things a bit? Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask you again, Mr. Hamill, to put a pause between the question and answer. And if you could slow down a little bit more, for the benefit of the court reporters and interpreters, when you speak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not something you have to apologise at all. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can I just interject to clear up another, as it were, variable. As I understand it, Colonel Hamill, even two identical mortars, fired with the same amount of charge and fired at the same angle, may result in a different impact point, even if fired at the same time, because of variations in the quality of the explosive mix, and also one mortar may have been fired many more times than the other mortar and the barrel may have been worn and the velocity of discharge may be reduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite correct in that. But, equally, it is possible to fire two rounds from the same tube within seconds of each other and have the rounds come down quite a distance away because of the fact that mortars are inherently an inaccurate weapon. There is a lot of variation even within the one weapon, in terms of firing. So you have what's called a beaten zone for the impacts from a specific mortar, and this tends to be an ellipse with a very long longitudinal pattern and a much less wide area. So it's like -- almost like an oval, and rounds can fall up to 10, 15, 20 metres away from each other within that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The French translation has only now been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel Hamill, we see here, theoretically, a minimum angle of 41.71 degrees. Do you agree that a maximum angle would be around 86 degrees?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In practical terms, probably. Theoretically, it is possible to fire a mortar at 90 degrees, but that would be extremely dangerous to the firer. You must also bear in mind, Dr. Karadzic, that a mortar bomb, when it lands, has a fairly wide area of destruction, as it were, so that it's not wise to fire too close to yourself, in case you get damaged. In the case of our 120-millimetre bomb, for example, the danger radius - radius, not diametre - is considered to be 500 metres. In the case of our 81-millimetre mortar, the danger radius is considered to be 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The real angle of descent was not determined here. A theoretical one was provided of 45.71 degrees. That is theory, and also if we take into account the buildings around the field and the maximum angle is 86 degrees. Do you agree that if the maximum angle is bigger and if it inclines towards 86 degrees, it speaks of the range from which the mortar was fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have already indicated to you that I do not agree that this was a mortar. If it was, however, it was fired from whatever angle, it doesn't really matter, because it's clear that whatever angle it was fired from would clear the buildings in Grbavica. So I'm afraid your question doesn't really make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please establish something now. The actually-established angle, does it speak of the range involved or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: There is no actually-established angle that I'm aware of. There is a minimum angle of descent of 45 -- 40.5 degrees, which was measured between the crater and the roof of the buildings in the appropriate direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since an angle was not actually established in real terms, why would I not say that it's 84, for instance? Where would it have been fired from if the angle of descent were 84?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I have no answer to that, as I don't have the range tables for the weapon in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on the basis of your experience, do you know that if the angle is obtuse, and you even said this today, it is probable that it would have been fired from a longer range? Analogously, the range would have to be shorter if the angle is bigger; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The higher the angle, the shorter the range in every case, and that goes for mortars and howitzers fired at high angle. It does not apply to guns, where the opposite effect occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we met up on the 12th of January this year, you said that the daily reports of the Lima 5 team could provide information about the activity of the team on that day, and you said that you had not been shown reports for that particular day. That goes for the Lima 5 team; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Insofar as my memory is accurate, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they tell you that the Bosnian investigators first carried out an investigation regarding this incident two and a half years after the incident actually occurred, that is to say, on the 21st of November, 1995, and that was done upon a request from this Tribunal, The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Nobody told me that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 09970; in e-court, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the previous question, while we are still waiting for this document: Colonel, how do people decide on a minimum angle, rather than a maximum angle? In other words, does this indicate a bit of a need to lengthen, as it were, the range towards the Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In general terms, when a crater analysis is being done particularly on mortars -- on mortar bombs, there is what's called a fuse tunnel, which is when the round hits the ground, particularly if the ground is hard, the explosion drives the fuse of the weapon directly forward. This creates a tunnel in which one can insert a stick, for example, and measure the angle of descent. I understand that that was not possible in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please focus on the first page. This is a document of the Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's P1699.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was established here -- or, rather, no, we can see the cover page here. And can we now have a look at page 3 of this document. Let's see if the English version is also page 3. In Serbian, it is 3. Yes, this is a record on this investigation two and a half years after the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't find that passage and couldn't interpret that part. Could you indicate where we can find that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to get to it now, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When this investigation was carried out by the Muslim investigators, the scene was shown to them by Refik Sokolar. According to the statement of this witness, and that is what was established during the investigation, itself, one projectile fell on the parking-lot, on the tarmac, and the other one fell on the soil surface next to the parking-lot. Is that what you were told as well, that one fell on the tarmac and the other one fell on soil, all on the parking-lot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: At this stage, I am not sure, to be quite honest. My memory would tell me that both fell on tarmac, but that may not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 says: "According to Witness Refik Sokolar ..." And so on and so forth. That is paragraph 4 in the Serbian version. And in the last paragraph in the Serbian version, it says that they didn't even look at the other one because two and a half years had elapsed and some plants were growing there, these two and a half years later. In English, it is actually the next page. Sorry. Actually, it's the last page, according to the -- it's the last paragraph here and then the next page in English, and we keep the same page in Serbian. So this investigation team that worked in 1995 - it's an investigation team of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina - says explicitly that the second shell did not fall on the tarmac, but, rather, it hit the ground, the soil, and they did not even investigate any further because there were some plants growing there by then. Can you see that part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we'll try to find it in English. In Serbian, it's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see this other crater?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you do speak of a second crater and the probability of the shell having been fired from the same direction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what I saw, that is what I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you concluded that only on the basis of one crater. How did you make any conclusions on the basis of a second crater that you never saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
