utterances.text: I did see two craters in that place at that time. I examined them both. One was quite clear. The second was more indistinct. The first one gave me a specific bearing. The second one looked very much to be as if it was coming from pretty much the same direction. No further can I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any explanation, then, how come, in 1995, there was only one crater in the tarmac, and in 2001, there were two?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at page 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness's answer is missing in the transcript. He said, No, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The microphone was not activated. But can you confirm that you said, No, Mr. Hamill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I said, No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to this photograph number 3, and may I inform you that this photograph comes from this investigation material of the Bosnian Muslim police. The 21st of November, 1995, is the date. Can you observe between the -- the contrast between the damaged surface and the undamaged surface? You see that this looks as if it happened only on the previous day. Can you agree with that, that there is a great deal of contrast?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I cannot comment on whether it looks like it was done the previous day or not. It certainly looks in very good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether this was one of the craters that you were shown during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I cannot say, because when I looked at the craters, as I said, they were filled with a red plasticised substance which preserved the general outlines of the crater but not necessarily every single detail. I would also say that given that a lot of time had passed, that there were certainly some erasure of detail, by effects of weather, by effects of human traffic, by whatever effects, just natural erosion, so I cannot say whether or not this is the same crater that I examined some years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this first crown forms an almost perfect circle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The inner crater is a perfect circle, almost, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would that be consistent with a bigger or a smaller angle of descent, this perfect circle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: This, in my view, would be from a higher angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that after the incident, the UNPROFOR also carried out an investigation and said in their report that two shells landed on a hard surface, or macadam, as they called it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a reference for that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's this previous document, P1053. That's where that paragraph is. I didn't want to repeat it. That's Crater 1 and Crater 2, P1053. If necessary, we can call it up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you satisfied, Ms. Edgerton, or do we have to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, not quite, Your Honours. And I'm struggling to find the reference, because I understand that document to say that one fell in the play area and one fell on the perimeter, which is somewhat different than two shells landing on a hard surface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see the document, then, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9. P1053, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention where it says that the shells landed on macadam and there is no fuse furrow that's -- therefore, the angle of descent and range could not be determined; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct, and that accords with my report, in which I state that both rounds fell on hard ground. And it seems to contradict the report you mentioned conducted by the personnel from the Presidency some time later. I would also draw your attention to the fact that this was conducted within five weeks of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is right. First, we have five weeks, then two and a half years, and then yours was six and a half years ago, wasn't it, from 1993 to 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11383 is the next 65 ter that we need. No, sorry, that's the same thing, except it's 65 ter. It's the same document. We don't need to call the other one up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, again, they determined 2400 mils and 500 mils. Do you agree that the UNPROFOR investigators determined a minimum angle of descent based on the height of the nearest building in the direction from which the shell came?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2569.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was looking at page 51, line 25. I don't think we have the right number of mils, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I thought the interpreters referred to those numbers. Could you check that the number of mils were correctly represented in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning one shell, the UNPROFOR determined 2400 mils, and the other one, 2.500. That was in the previous document we showed. One was not 2400, but 2.420, and the other one was 2500. It's from P1053, the document produced by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this image, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Firstly, in relation to your first question, we've already established what the mils were and the minimum angle of descent. I think that goes back quite a number of pages. In relation to this image, it looks to me like a scene from Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the playground in question, and the parking-lot is to the right of the playground, so we can't see it in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Again, I neither agree nor disagree. Given, as you mentioned, that my investigation took place about nine years ago, my memory would not retain such detail. But it certainly looks, generally, as if it could be that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We show this photograph mainly to show the height of these buildings. Do you remember that from three sides, south, east, and west, the buildings were approximately this height?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the angle of descent depends, in a certain measure, from the height of these buildings and the distance between the buildings and the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly. Pythagorus proved that a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of those two craters that you were shown, you established that the direction was 2200 mils, plus/minus 50, and that made you determine that the direction was Toplik?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that there were certain traces of shrapnel in the shape of fins, and that that made you think it was a gun, not a howitzer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The wings -- there were wings, not fins, on the ground at the time, and that made me think that it was a gun or howitzer, not a mortar. A gun and a howitzer, in effect, fires the same shell, or at least the same type of shell, so the effect on the ground would be pretty similar. A mortar bomb is very different in its construction, and, as a result, would have a different impact on the ground, and this would be very apparent in a fresh crater. It would not be so apparent in an old crater. And the longer time went on, clearly, the more degraded a crater will get and the less it will retain the qualities that it would have had originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did, in fact, say exactly what you said. If we just changed "the shape of fins" in the record to "the shape of wings," your answer could have been, It's correct. I did say "wings." That was interpreted to you as "fins." That caused the confusion. Let's see all the conclusions and determinations that were made in relation to these craters. First of all, in the investigation of the Muslim team, photograph number 3, do you see those wings? You remember it, a perfect circle, a high angle of descent, or perhaps you were shown a different crater?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I could see the wings. Perhaps you mightn't, not being a professional artillery officer, but I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us see. The UNPROFOR determined 2.420 and 2.500 mils. The Bosnian investigators determined that the shell came from south-east, that is to say, 100 [as interpreted] degrees from the azimuth, that is, from the north. That would be 1.955 mils, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No. What you must remember is that a mil is an artificial construction, and those of us who have been trained, as I have, will use 6.400 mils in a circle, for ease of calculation. Clearly, one-quarter is 1.600, one-eighth is 800, and so on. However, other establishments use a different number of mils, some could use 6.000, some use 6.230, which is more accurate in the sense of it relates to Pi, in actual fact, and the subtention of difference at distance, so I cannot say that it would be 1.955. From my perspective and in my training, 100 degrees would be 1.788, approximately. But, again, you have to examine: What do we mean by the azimuth? And, again, where I look at it from is I look at grid north, not magnetic north and not true north. We use a grid on a map so that everybody is playing on the same field, as it were. So I cannot compare, specifically, without knowing where those investigators were coming from, firstly, how many mils they have in a circle and, secondly, what north they were using and from what map. I was using the standard map that we had in UNPROFOR, which was gridded on a UTM system. What they were using, I don't know. But the likelihood is that it was probably somewhere in the same general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They wrote that it was 110 degrees from the north to the south-east. If 100 were 1700 mils, then 110 degrees would be, as they concluded, 1.955 mils. Obviously, they were using similar parameters to yours. It's not 100, so it's not 1700 mils; it's, instead, 110 degrees, so it's 1955. You determined that it was up to 2.350, and the UNPROFOR decided it was 2.420 and 2.500. Do you see that nothing is consistent here with anything else? If it's easier for you, we can call up 65 ter 9970.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Going back to line 20 in page 54, I presume it is, the translation said "100 degrees." That is from the north, that would be 1955. So it is clear that there was a slight error in the transcript. 1.955 is, more or less, something in the region of 110 degrees, from my perspective as well, yes. In relation to 1.955, in relation to 2.400, it actually isn't a huge amount. It sounds large, but it's not. 1 mil at 1.000 metres subtends 1 metre, so it isn't a huge amount. If the range was, say, 3.000, then 1 mil makes a difference of 3 metres, that's all. Forty mils makes a difference of 120 metres at 3.000. What I'm getting at here is that, as Judge Morrison said earlier on, weapons can be fired on the same bearing at the same angle, and due to slight differences in the composition of the explosive charge, in the air temperature, in the wind direction and speed, in charge temperature and so on, a round will not fall, necessarily, in the same place. Lightning doesn't hit twice, as they say. It is not going to fall into the same hole. So this variation, while apparently large, is not perhaps as large as you might think. They're all pretty much in the same area; that is, somewhere in east of south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you agree that the confrontation lines were close to one another and that they were at a distance from this place of -- how much? What is the information that you were given? How far were the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The confrontation lines were fairly close in that area, and, in fact, they were within, I suppose, 50 to 100 metres of each other, I would say. It was one block of buildings to the next in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that from this pitch to the confrontation lines, the distance was about 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Probably. Sorry, to the armija line. Clearly, the VRS line was further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the minimum distance from which one can fire an 82-millimetre mortar with a zero charge, let's say? If it would be of assistance, I can put up firing tables on the screen. 1D2262. In other words, do you agree that with a zero charge, the minimum distance from which an 82-millimetre mortar can be fired is about 80 metres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It can be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here is the table, if you need it, but I believe you know it by heart, and you have confirmed that. Is it helpful?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. At charge zero, clearly it's 80 metres is the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the angle of descent would then be around 85 degrees; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The angle of ascent is certainly 85 degrees. I don't see an angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the fourth column? Sorry, column 9, that's the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. It's "1421."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at this line, "300 metres"? What would the angle of descent be then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is somewhat obscured by the letter -- or by the number "0," but it looks as though it's "12" something "2."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, in any case, you do agree that if the angle were around 85 degrees, then the pattern of the traces would be close to a perfect circle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: They would still have the characteristics of a mortar bomb explosion, which they don't appear to have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just on the transcript, line 24, page 57, I thought I heard the interpreter say "85 degrees," instead of "125 degrees ," but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. We were about to correct that ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the maximum angle of descent is about 86 degrees. The maximum degree is achieved from a minimum distance; is that true, Lieutenant-Colonel? The smaller the distance, the bigger the angle? That's what you told us today .

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the bigger the angle, then the pattern of fragment traces is closer to a perfect circle. That's what the first column shows us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In the case of a shell, yes, that is correct. In the case of a mortar bomb, you would have a serious undercut on the front of the crater and you would have a line almost perpendicular -- in fact, perpendicular to the incoming angle, and I didn't see those on this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want to see that photograph again, photo number 3?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: If you wish to see it, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 09970, that's 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I remind you, Mr. Karadzic, that this document we just saw, in relation to the table of charges, was marked for identification until we are satisfied as to the origin of it, so it's still pending.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's part of the manual, the official JNA manual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we know that. It's for you to up-load that and inform the Chamber to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And also we need the translation, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that we called up has one. But if you mean the translation of the table, we'll provide one. The upper photograph, number 3, please. The previous page. We see number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This first crown, Lieutenant-Colonel, does it form an almost perfect circle?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it does so appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would these be traces of a mortar or a howitzer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Clearly, I would like to actually see the crater physically. But judging from the photograph, it looks to me as if it is from a shell; that is, from a howitzer or from a gun. Probably a howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Could I also say I have no idea of the scale of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope that this measuring stick actually serves for measurement and the dividers are at intervals of a metre, that that's what the investigating team used. Tell us, please, whether the range can be approximately determined if we know the calibre of the shell from the moment when we hear the explosion and from the moment we hear the firing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: There are possibilities, using sound-ranging equipment, to determine the origin of a shell. There was not such equipment available to us in Sector Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, for instance, if eye-witnesses first heard the sound of firing and then the explosion, we could -- on the basis of what we know about the speed of sound, we could come to a conclusion regarding the range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: If the eye-witnesses were present and saw the explosion, and were close enough to it and heard the sound of the firing after that, and could work out in their heads at that stage the distance involved, then certainly you could work out the range, yes. It would be inexact, but it would give an approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the time between the firing and the explosion or impact would be of certain significance, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that two eye-witnesses heard the sound of firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, could we have a reference for that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll provide the statements of these witnesses. I was just interested in the opinion of the lieutenant-colonel about that particular matter, and I was interested in hearing whether he had been informed about everything, whether he had received all information which was indispensable for him to make conclusions. We are going to supply the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. We can carry on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Richard Higgs, a Prosecution expert, visited this location somewhat after you did, the 12th of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in that sense, you wouldn't know about his findings, would you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if it's of any assistance -- actually, 65 ter 10083 would be the number. Can we call that up, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HIGGS SAYS
utterances.text: "At the request of the International Tribunal, I visited the location with Mr. Chester Stamp and I examined two craters, the two craters concerned. Both craters are filled with a red substance, which makes an analysis impossible now. However, a sufficient part of the calibre has still been preserved, and certain findings can be made." Have you found that somewhere on page 8?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we seeing the correct page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm not sure, in English, whether it is 8 or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's probably page 7.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: C. [Interpretation] "At the request of the International Tribunal," that's what it says in Serbian, and it's on the top of the page in Serbian. It's page number 7 in English: [In English] "At the request of the Tribunal, I visited ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know that Mr. Higgs also included that this was a mortar shell? UNPROFOR investigators, in P0 -- or P1053, came to the conclusion that it was a mortar shell. The Muslim police investigators came to the conclusion that it was a mortar shell. Your position is that it is more probable that it is a gun or howitzer. Do you have any explanation for such discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: The explanation I would give you is that a considerable period of time elapsed before I conducted my investigation, but regardless of whether it was a gun or a mortar, the direction of fire was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that if you look at any directions, the two armies are facing each other at the lines?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to ascertain responsibility, would it be necessary to pin-point the range, to determine the range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the Markale incident, you came somewhat later, didn't you, some six or seven days after the incident; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. The incident took place on the 5th of February, and I first saw it on the 10th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you said to us, and when you testified in the case of General Galic, that whoever was firing would have to be very lucky to hit a place like the Markale Market is with a single shell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reference?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that the lieutenant-colonel could confirm that even without the transcript. The 26th of March, 2002, is the date of the transcript. 6218 is the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, in the sense that if they were intending to hit the Markale Market, to fire one round and get what we call a target round from a mortar, from a 120-millimetre mortar, from a distance would be amazing, good luck for the gunner, and horrendous bad luck for those who were standing where the round went off, because to hit a target from a mortar takes a lot of effort, you need a lot of preparatory information on possibly firing, and you need to fire very, very specifically on data that has been acquired normally from adjusting rounds. That was one round that was fired on that day that we are aware of in that general area, and for it to be a target round was absolutely amazing, if Markale was the target. Line 1, "for it to be a target round," yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly look at 65 ter 10336, and then in that document, page 161. 10336 is the number, and 161 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what you were speaking of. You had certain reservations, in view of the intentions, or, rather, you thought that whoever was firing had not intended to fire on Markale; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I didn't mean that; specifically, if he, who was firing, intended to hit Markale, he was extremely lucky, from his perspective. What I said was that -- what I intended was that it may not have been directly at Markale, but it was certainly in the general area of the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Tell me, if I can just extrapolate from that, what you're saying is this: that for a round to have landed where it did, it must have been, as a matter of common sense, fired in that general direction, but where it exactly landed was a matter of chance, given that there was only one shot and no ranging fire beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A great deal of luck and also an absence of willingness to hit precisely that point where the shell had landed; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Wrong. I am not saying there was an absence of willingness to hit precisely that point where the shell had landed. I do not know where it was -- at which point it was aimed, but it was certainly aimed at an area full of civilians in the center of Sarajevo. It hit an area which was crowded with civilians. Whether by chance or design, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a technical adviser in this case, and during the mandate of the investigation team, investigations complemented the previous investigations that had been carried out by the UN; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I would suggest that the investigation that we conducted superseded the previous investigations that had been carried out by the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to have a break. We'll have a break for half an hour and then resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you received an assignment from the United Nations to carry out this subsequent examination, using the relevant physical evidence and findings, to determine responsibility for this incident; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: You attempt to determine responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I call up in e-court the previous document, 11036, pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the traces you found were tiny and not usable for analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Mirza Jamakovic offered fragments to you, and you refused them because there was no proof they originated from the site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I'm not aware that a Mirza Jamakovic offered fragments to us, but we were certainly offered fragments by the Presidency side liaison officer, and we refused them, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 37 in this document, please, 65 ter 10336. That's the transcript from 2002, page 37 in the transcript -- that's to say in the document, but in the transcript, it's 6094, straddling 6095. Beginning with line 18, somebody asks whether Jamakovic -- in fact, you say that somebody contacted you, and you were offered fragments, but your team refused them. Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see that here, and you said you had no evidence that they originate from the scene. The determination was somehow made of the direction from which the shells could have come, and you established there were six possible places in that direction from which the shell could have been fired. Two of them were closer on Muslim territory, and four of them were more distant on Serb territory. Correct? Can we see, in the same document, page 135. In the document itself, it's 135, and in the transcript, it's 6192. Is it true you determined there were six possible places from which the shell could have been fired?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also established that it was more likely to have been fired from a position closer to Markale?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's towards the bottom of the previous page or the top of this page. Could we see the previous page. The next page, then, please. The bottom of this page, your answer is, in line 23: [In English] "The probability would be slightly higher the nearer the target is to the weapon. But not much. You're looking at approximately equal times of flight because ..." And so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yeah, I see that, but you're misreading it, I'm afraid. This has nothing whatsoever to do with the probability that the round was fired from a closer position. It is in relation to the probability that a target round would be achieved earlier from a closer position, because clearly the bomb hasn't as far to travel, is not likely to be deflected by wind, is -- generally, it's going to have a smaller pattern on the ground. So if it is going to be a target round, it's clearly going to be easier from a shorter range, but that has nothing to do with the probability that the round was actually fired from any one of the six positions. The probability was equal from all of them, technically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in case this place was deliberately targeted, you are assigning a higher likelihood to positions that are nearer? Regarding the intention to hit that place, if such an intent exists, it's more likely to achieve that goal from a nearer position than from a more distant one. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In one sense, yes. But you were connecting two items which don't belong together. You're connecting technical accuracy with intent, and I am not doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just following up on what you said, that if the intent existed, it must have been pure luck to hit the target, the desired target, with just one projectile. But let's move on. You said that possible ranging in and adjusting the aim would have had any value within two hours only, and if two hours had passed, then these same parameters would no longer apply?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Again, that is correct, we do accept that targets which are adjusted have a two-hour validity. Now, this obviously changes in relation to conditions at a specific time in a specific place, but we accept, from our technical point of view, that two hours is the window of opportunity, if you could put it that way. But going back to what you said earlier on about the beaten zone, it is a fact that the beaten zone, as we call it, in other words, where the mortar bomb lands, is smaller if the range is smaller. The further out you go, Your Honours, clearly, the bigger the discrepancy is going to be, because the round will be affected by more factors, but that does not mean anything in relation to intent. That is purely a technical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, then, that ranging in months beforehand would have been pointless; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that ranging in from a different location would be useless for a third location, as it were? So if a weapon is at one location, ranging in for a different location is pointless?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It is possible to use adjusted fire data from a different location, providing certain parameters are met. These would include the fact that it's pointing generally in the same direction and it's within a reasonable distance and within our two-hour time-frame. But with mortars, it is more difficult than it is with guns to transfer this data because of the inherent inaccuracy of a non-rifled barrel, which is what most mortars have, they have non-rifled barrels. It is possible, in limited circumstances, to use data.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, ranging in, say, from Lukavica would not have been useful for a weapon from the north-east, so from the north-east, Mirkovci, where they say that this shell came from; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the point of impact, there was a tunnel, and there was the stabiliser, the tail-fin, right, that was sticking out of the ground? Actually, finding the direction using a compass is possible, but that is not a fully accurate method because it was done a week after the explosion; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I disagree. It was accurate, because the fuse tunnel was still -- in effect, still intact. The mortar area, the markings on the ground, were intact. There was a continuity of evidence for the full week between the shelling on the 5th and the time we arrived and did our crater analysis on the 11th. So the continuity of evidence gave us the opportunity to do an accurate check on where the round was fired from, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're not talking about distance; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not talking about distance. I am talking about bearing or direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Colonel Hamill, I know it's going back a little bit, and it's probably very self-evident, but it seems to me important that it's in evidence. One of the things that's going to affect a mortar round, particularly if it's fired at a trajectory that sends it higher rather than lower, is going to be the wind. Now, I understand, and perhaps you can confirm from your experience, that the higher the mortar round goes, the more it's going to be -- and the longer it's in flight, the more the prevailing wind is going to affect it, and that upper winds can be stronger and, indeed, blowing in a different direction than winds that are observable at ground level. Is that a correct analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is precisely correct, again, Your Honour. Thank you for the clarification. It is clear that the higher up the round goes, it goes from a greater distance. Therefore, it passes through different envelopes of air, as it were, in which wind speeds and directions cannot be determined from the ground without the use of, for example, weather balloons. So as it goes up, it can change direction right or left, forward or backwards. It can be retarded or it can be advanced, in a sense, as it goes through the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And, therefore, the only way to predict where a round is going to fall is by observing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: -- previous ranging rounds, and even then it's a guesstimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Particularly so with mortars, it is a guesstimate, with guns which are much more accurate due to the design of the weapon and due to the design of the shell, which fits into the barrel much more closely than it does with a mortar bomb, then you have a lot more accuracy. This is why guns are more accurate and why mortars are considered to be area-suppressing weapons as opposed to targeting weapons. That is the case. You have to adjust the fire, and you must adjust within a short space of time, and it takes some time -- normally, it can take three or five or more rounds to adjust on to a target which you want to hit subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And earlier you mentioned that mortars were, by and large, non-rifled weapons, although I think some rifled mortars do exist, and "rifling" is the grooves in the barrel which spin a projectile in order to counteract external forces and to make the -- ballistically make the round more accurate. But this is likely to have been fired from a non-rifled barrel, and, therefore, even more subject to the vagaries of external forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This was a thin-stabilised round as opposed to a spin-stabilised round. Guns fire spin-stabilised rounds. As you mentioned, the rifling in the barrel spins the shell to give it its direction. Now, that brings in its own effects. It normally spins it slightly to the right. With mortars, with the tail-fin which they have, it is the tail-fin which gives it the stabilisation, which stops it from wobbling -- literally, wobbling in the air and which keeps it in its direction. However, it doesn't stop it entirely from wandering and it will wander. And this is why, as I say, the mortar is a more inherently inaccurate weapon than a gun. There are, certainly, rifled mortars, but in my experience, there weren't any in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm going to skip that part, because it was clarified and explained so well. Can we now have page 27 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on line 11: [In English] "Now, on page 3 of that document, item 17, there is a finding in respect to culpability. The last three lines read: 'There is insufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb. The mortar bomb in question could have been fired from either side.' Was that your finding?" [Interpretation] And now your answer: "That was our finding. That is an accurate assessment." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to discuss angles anymore, because these are final conclusions. Also, there were traces indicating that the crater had been tampered with between the two analyses, and that that also impeded measurements; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [In English] I would not say that the crater was tampered with, per se. What happened was that one team withdrew the tail-fin, which certainly changed slightly the crater, and particularly the fuse tunnel. It was not tampering; it was an attempt to do a crater analysis and find out from where the round had come. So my understanding was that UNPROFOR had, in effect, secured the market area from a few minutes after the round fell until our team arrived on site. It was on that basis that we conducted our investigation and made our findings of fact, not speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that when we met during that interview, you confirmed to us that you never saw any wounded or dead people from Markale 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I so confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agreed, didn't we, that such a large number of wounded and killed persons in such a small area was something which you also found to be suspicious a bit; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I certainly made some speculations as we were having our discussions. That is not the same as stating facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you, Colonel, whether you knew what the deployment was of Muslim forces within the city, itself, as well as where their headquarters were and the deployment of their mortars, guns and tanks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I had no knowledge, personally, of the deployment of their mortars, guns, and tanks at any specific time. In relation to the deployment of the armija forces within the city, I was aware, in general terms, of where they were. I certainly knew where their headquarters was. I knew the barracks they were located in. But specific individual items did not stay in place for very long, if you're referring to, for example, mortars, guns, and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In contrast to the Serbs, as you confirmed through your observations, the Muslim Army often changed their positions. They had mortars either on trucks or they changed their positions, as such. You observed that the Serbs mostly had stationary weapons, they did not move them; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: In general times -- in general terms, the VRS did not move their heavy weapons. They kept them in situ, which made it very easy to keep an eye on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the southern part of Sarajevo, you saw Serb artillery positions. When the Serbs wanted to fire their mortars or use their other artillery pieces, they informed the monitors of their intention, they would mention what their targets would be, and they asked whether the monitors wanted to observe that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That certainly happened on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in that sense, the Army of Republika Srpska was not firing without the knowledge of the UN observers, but the observers could not always verify whether that was the target that the Serbs had notified them of; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It was not always the case that the VRS fired with the knowledge of UN observers, because we didn't always have observers present. We certainly didn't have observers present in a lot of the firing positions that the VRS had either south or north of the city. On occasions, we were asked to send observers so that we could examine the firing and confirm the firing. This was normally done when the VRS was responding to an attack by the armija. On occasions, because of the small number of observers that we had, firing was conducted that we had not prior information on. At one stage, south of the city, I had a total of five observers for a city the size of Sarajevo. This was simply -- it was not possible, physically, to cover every VRS position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many observers did you have altogether on the Serb side, how many such locations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: We had a number of different locations, and I could go through them, but give or take, say, about -- about eight, approximately eight positions in the summer of 1993, each of which should have had a minimum of two observers and possibly up to a maximum of about five. Now, given that situations changed on a daily basis in relation to not just Sarajevo, but also the rest of Bosnia and Croatia and Macedonia and, indeed, Serbia, where we had observers, observers were continually moving. Observers had a need to have leave, there was illness, so on a daily basis the situation changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And am I right if I say that you had three or four times more observers on Serb territory in Sarajevo than in Muslim territory? On the Serb territory, you had up to 11 observers, and on Muslim territory, you had 3, right, and this includes the northern part of the front?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is incorrect. We had five teams on the Papa side and we had, as I said, about eight teams or nine teams, something like that, on the Lima side. The Papa side teams were pretty much the same size as ours, but you must bear in mind that they were covering a much smaller area. They were compacted within the city and they were spread throughout it from the west to the east, so they covered, certainly, less area than our teams on the outside did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 622 -- actually, it is page 6222 in the transcript, and we'll see what document it is. Or within the document, itself, 165 of the document, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to 15, 16, and 17, those lines of your answer: [In English] "But would always claim, of course, that it was a military target, and there would be no way of verifying what was on the other side." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Serbs, who are notified that there would be fire on a certain target, are unable to check with their colleagues from the other side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you referring to the UNMOs who are working on the Lukavica side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your response, beginning with 11: [In English] "So they told us what they were firing at. They told us perhaps it was in response to an attack on certain positions or certain villages or areas. Invariably, the firers would tell the team which would be supervising them, as it were, which would be monitoring team that they were firing at -- what they were firing at. But would always claim, of course, that it was a military target, and there would be no way of verifying what was on the other side." [Interpretation] Do you accept that the Serbs thought that you were able to check it with your colleagues on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I neither accept nor reject that fact. It is just in line 21, you say: "Do you agree that the Serbs who were notified that there would be fire on a certain target ..." This is why I asked were you referring to the UNMOs who were working on the VRS side, but I certainly stand by the fact, as stated in the previous case at lines 11 to 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's not correctly interpreted in line 21. It's correct on page 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs would notify something. They would say they would be shooting at such and such military target for such and such a reason. My assumption is that they were unable to know that you had no way of checking whether that was, indeed, the target. In July 1993, you heard about attacks on the UN humanitarian convoy from Hrasnica and Igman, a territory that was under the control of the BH Army, and that resulted in civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just wondering if there was actually a question after the first paragraph at page 78, lines 21 to 24.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I received the answer, that the lieutenant-colonel could not either confirm nor deny what the Serbs knew, and my theory is that the Serbs were unable to know that the UN observers were unable to verify their assertions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- interject, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just as an explanation of the way we worked at the time, in order to clarify the matter for the Court, the observers on the Papa side, the Presidency side, and there were observers on the Lima side, the Lukavica headquarters of the VRS, and we had two types of reports. We had shootreps and increps. A shootrep was when we were -- when the people alongside whom we were working, whether they were VRS or armija, were firing. An increp was an incoming, it was an incident report of firing coming in. Now, my teams on the VRS side reported shootreps of items going out and we reported increps of items coming in, explosions within our area. Similarly, the Papa side did exactly the same thing, and on a daily basis this was correlated into a report by Sector Sarajevo headquarters. So you had, perhaps, any correlation being done at that level. From our perspective, we were too busy reporting these incidents and conducting our patrols and interviewing people and attempting to implement cease-fires to do the processing of the information, as such, but I'm sure it was done at a higher level than ours. And certainly every increp and every shootrep that was sent in went to both sides and went to the headquarters, and, again, on a daily basis formed part of our daily situation report from Sector Sarajevo both to BiH Command and on to UNPROFOR HQ. So there is the possibility of correlating rounds minute by minute from where they were fired to where they landed where it was known. But, again, Your Honours, I must emphasise that our numbers were small and we did not always either hear or see shootings or shellings going on or incoming explosions or attacks. We did not always see it. I hope this is of some benefit to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hamill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, in any case, you had observers on the Serb side, and you had more of them on the Serb side than on the Papa side? At least you had more stations, if not more staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement from December 1995, given from 13 through 15 December 1995, on page 4 you said that the Serbs, before using their artillery, would inform the observers of their intentions. That's the reference to the statement, and the other references are to your earlier testimony. Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly do, but I think I qualified it by saying that that was certainly the case in Lima 5, in particular, not necessarily everywhere. On the northern side of the city, the VRS was much more secretive than the brigades on the south side, where we seemed to have a better rapport, if you will. In the north, we had huge problems getting information from the brigades. We also had problems in freedom of movement in the northern sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your colleagues on Muslim territory have testified here and said, again, that they had considerable restrictions of movement. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Anecdotally, yes. But from personal experience, clearly not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 119 from the previous document, where we can see references to this attack from Hrasnica and Dobrinja against the humanitarian convoy and civilian targets. The question is in line 7, and you answer in line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the page? You say you heard of an incident -- of these incidents, that there have been shootings from the Muslim side in Hrasnica and Dobrinja, causing civilian casualties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: It says "Hrasnica and Igman." And, yes, I heard of the incident, but as I say there on line 18, I had no personal knowledge of it. It allegedly happened before my time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case -- in fact, that's your statement from 1995. You said you never eye-witnessed the deliberate attack on civilian targets during your tenure in Lima 5 and Lima 8. There was a lot of combat activity between the two sides, and there were cases when the VRS shelled Hrasnica and Mount Igman as a result of incoming fire from the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Army from their territory. [In English] Witness statement December 13 to 15, 1995, page 3. [Interpretation] Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I certainly said it. It was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were staying in Lukavica, you experienced fire coming from the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. We experienced both mortar fire and sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you had a good relationship with the populous and the Army of Republika Srpska members with whom you had contact in that area of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you established that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina used its mortars close to the UN headquarters and also from the locality of Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: So I was told. I never personally saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On 26th May 1993, the BH Army attacked from the area of Hrasnica and Igman, a civilian area in Serb territory, with 82-millimetre mortars at 10.58. They fired 13 rounds, as well as infantry fire, while the VRS responded at 11.40 with 10 shells. We can take a look at that. It's your statement from December 5, on page 4. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I don't recall saying it specifically, but I'm not surprised. I could well have said it because such events certainly occurred around that time. I cannot now state specifically it was the 26th of May, but it was within a day or two of that, so it is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On 19 July 1993, the BH Army, at Igman, launched a major attack against Ilidza -- against the Ilidza and Igman Brigades of the VRS, and the VRS responded. Commander Cojic of the Igman Brigade of the VRS re-took Igman from the BH Army in a counter-offensive, and the United Nations forced a cease-fire and started patrolling that area; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that point, as soon as the UN withdrew from danger, Igman started changing hands? Do you recall saying that when you were testifying in the Galic case - on page 612 [as interpreted] - at one point the United Nations withdrew, and Mount Igman -- or at least that part of Mount Igman changed hands, the BH Army took it again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That did happen, yes. The UNPROFOR troops withdrew from certain positions. There was an agreement between armija, VRS, and the UN that no positions would change. However, the armija did occupy positions that the UN had previously been in. They moved forward, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's page 155 in the previous document, dated 26 March 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a major crisis occurred in the relationship between the VRS and the UNPROFOR because the BH Army made an unauthorised entry into the territory that the Serbs had handed over to the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do so remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1993, you went to Kiseljak to attend a conference, and then you moved to the Papa side. You saw the Kosevo Hospital, and you saw two nurses and one doctor killed by a shell. You also saw a hole in a wall over 1 metre in diametre, forming almost a perfect circle. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is almost correct. I didn't see any nurses or a doctor killed. I was informed, when we were there, that there had been those casualties when the building was hit by a shell, but that had happened some time before and I don't know when. I did see the hole in the wall. It was a large one, and it was almost a perfect circle. So, yes, that part is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 128 of this document, please, to see your conclusion to the effect that according to the position of the hole and its orientation, your conclusion was that it was more likely to have been caused by fire from the city -- from the Muslim side than from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In our discussion, we have agreed that during your briefings, you had been warned that Muslim forces in town could very well have placed dead bodies in crime scenes and such things; that kind of warning was present among UN staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One shelling incident involving Kosevo Hospital looked like it originated from a Muslim Army tank positioned north of the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: But, of course, I didn't use the expression "a Muslim Army tank." I don't use that kind of expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whatever, that's what you call it. But we, too, are Bosnians, and we get angry that this attribute, "Bosnian," is being monopolised. We Serbs and Croats are also Bosnians. However, did you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: And Montenegrins as well, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was your view that the Muslim side, or Bosnian side, if you wish, took political advantage of incidents and that these incidents frequently occurred at the same time as various international conferences were convened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was certainly my view, my opinion, yes. But it was my personal opinion, as such, not a UN position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we may need to complete the transcript, in terms of your answer which was not translated because of the overlapping. Probably you answered in B/C/S, but which was not caught by the court reporter. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also suggested, Your Honour, that Montenegrins might also wish to be considered as Bosnians in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not all, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was only with regard to the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you saw for yourself that the VRS was made up of soldiers who virtually lived on the front-line, or very close to the front-line, rather than in barracks, as a professional army would. It was a popular army made up of locals who lived there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That was absolutely, without a doubt, true. The vast majority of people that I met in the VRS in the SRK area were locals, they were living in Kasindol and Gornji Kotorac, in Vojkovici. Many of them had come from the center of the city, from Skenderija, from Novo Sarajevo, from other places, and as refuges. They were locals, in the main. There were, of course, a sprinkling of people from other parts, Serbia, Montenegro, but mostly they were locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you did not know the precise deployment of these units within Sarajevo, I mean, ABiH units or their staffs or their headquarters and firing positions, you agreed that these were legitimate military targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Within a war, there are such a thing as legitimate military targets, and they are military units and installations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are fully aware of the disproportion, in terms of the number of soldiers, and you noted that the VRS used its artillery efficiently in order to repel and offset this advantage on the BH Army side, in terms of numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it was quite clear that the number of soldiers on the armija side was much greater, in infantry terms, than the number of soldiers on the VRS side, so the VRS used their artillery as what we call a force multiplier. In other words, they used their artillery to offset the fact and overcome the fact that they were inferior in actual numbers of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that there were attacks -- infantry attacks by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the Lukavica-Pale road, and that many persons got killed there? 130 soldiers, those were the figures. Do you remember these losses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: I remember, specifically at the end of May 1993, there was such an attack uphill against the road running from Lukavica to Pale, and I remember hearing from the Presidency side, from our UNMOs on the Presidency side, that in excess of 100 soldiers were killed from the armija, as opposed to, if memory serves me right, about 3 soldiers from the VRS, who were in prepared positions on the hillside looking down on these troops who were attempting to assault them with absolutely no covering fire and no preparatory bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you could have observed that the Serb side did not control, for example, all of Ilidza or all of Vogosca, but only the Serb areas? For example, Hrasnica is the Muslim part of Ilidza, and Hrasnica was under Muslim control; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: My understanding was that places like Hrasnica and Ilidza were mixed before the war. I did not see them like that. Certainly, there was a huge amount of population movement, so that by the time I got there, Hrasnica was exclusively manned by Bosnian Muslims, and Ilidza was divided between the Serb and Croat population and the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the interview, when we met up, you agreed that lines went through the city, itself, and that the line was basically divided during the course of the war, and these lines were stable during your tour there, they didn't change very much; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. The lines were effectively static during my period. And in the former Yugoslavia from May 1993 until July 1994, there was very little change in the Sarajevo city area, very little.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I sincerely thank you for meeting with the Defence and for testifying here. I would like to conclude at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. Edgerton, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only one very small point, Your Honours, and that comes from transcript line -- or page 85, lines 22 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there, Lieutenant-Colonel, Dr. Karadzic asked you the following: "Although you did not know the whether precise deployment -- did not know the precise deployment of these units within Sarajevo, I mean, ABiH units or their staffs or their headquarters and firing positions, you agreed that these were legitimate military targets; correct?" And your response was: "Within a war, there are such a thing as legitimate military targets, and they are military units and installations, yes." Do you remember that question and answer that was just a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was just a little bit confused, because I have always understood that the definition of "military targets" depends on a number of factors. Did you mean, actually, to define "military objects" rather than "military targets"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN HAMILL
utterances.text: They are military objects. I didn't want to expand too much. But military targets are objects which, in effect, give an advantage to one side or the other by way of physical or moral cybernetic advantage. So a military target is, of course, much larger in scope than just units and headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Lieutenant-Colonel Hamill. I thank you, on behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? We would like to tender the pages that -- oh, now I hear that the entire document has been admitted, so I don't have to tender individual pages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, is it practicable to go into the next witness or shall we adjourn for today?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually have to say that the next witness, Mr. Begic, was not able to leave Bosnia, due to weather conditions, and, therefore, he is not available today. And we -- I have spoken to Mr. Robinson, and it is my understanding that Dr. Karadzic agrees to have Mr. Bell as the next witness, and I think it's much more practical to have him start tomorrow morning instead of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then probably that's it for today. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just take a moment to make an objection for the record concerning Mr. Bell's testimony, if you would allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As you know, we have previously objected to the testimony of war correspondents and received a very negative reaction from the Chamber on that. But, nevertheless, because we do think that it may be an issue on appeal, we would like to move to exclude Mr. Bell's testimony since he is a retired war correspondent, and it remains our position that he is not capable of waiving the war correspondent privilege, so for the record I make that motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you know the Chamber's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very clearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Negative, albeit correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I take this opportunity to raise this: Probably parties are aware of the recent development, in terms of amendment of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; in particular, regarding the judicial notice of authenticity of the documentary evidence. So if the parties want to make a further submission on that issue, that will be allowed. By the end of this week, is it practicable? I don't think it's practicable to make a ruling on that issue before the recess, but I would appreciate if we could have that submission, well, at least before the beginning of the next year. That should be possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Are you referring to the current motion that's pending regarding the intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's correct. You'll have some time to respond to the Prosecution -- a week to respond to the Prosecution's submission, if at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.09 p.m.,
